divide.name: Darboux sums and the definition of integrability
divide.brief: This part sets up the Riemann integral for bounded functions on a closed interval [a,b]: partitions and refinements, upper and lower Darboux sums, the lemma that refining a partition raises lower sums and lowers upper sums, and that every lower sum is at most every upper sum. It defines the upper and lower integrals as an infimum and a supremum, defines a function as Riemann integrable when they are equal, and proves the Riemann (epsilon) criterion: f is integrable if and only if for every epsilon > 0 there is a partition with U(f,P) - L(f,P) < epsilon. Worked examples computed from the definition (constant functions, a step function, f(x) = x or x^2 on [0,1]) and the Dirichlet function as a bounded function that is not integrable. It ends by mentioning Riemann sums with tags and the mesh definition as an equivalent definition, without developing the proof. Edges: proofs that whole classes of functions (continuous, monotone, Thomae's function) are integrable belong to 'Which functions are integrable'. Properties such as linearity and additivity belong to 'Properties of the integral'. Supremum, infimum and their epsilon characterisation come from 'The real numbers' and are used, not retaught. What matters for this learner: the integral is defined by a supremum and an infimum, so the sup/inf skills from 'The real numbers' are exercised here; integrability is something to prove; and the Riemann criterion is the working tool used by every later proof in the integral.

divide.name: Which functions are integrable
divide.brief: This part uses the Riemann criterion to prove that important classes of functions are integrable on [a,b]: continuous functions (via uniform continuity, the Heine-Cantor theorem from 'Limits of functions and continuity'), monotone functions (via a uniform partition and a telescoping sum), bounded functions with finitely many discontinuities (by isolating the bad points in short intervals), and Thomae's function as an integrable function with infinitely many (countably many, dense) discontinuities, with integral 0. It contrasts Thomae's function with the Dirichlet function (defined and shown non-integrable in 'Darboux sums and the definition of integrability'). It closes by stating Lebesgue's criterion (a bounded function is Riemann integrable exactly when its set of discontinuities has measure zero), with measure zero defined by covers of small total length, without proof, as a pointer to 'Where analysis leads'. Edges: the definition and the Riemann criterion come from the previous sibling. Integrability of sums, products and compositions with continuous functions belongs to 'Properties of the integral'. Uniform continuity is proved in 'Limits of functions and continuity' and only used. What matters for this learner: seeing how one criterion turns into proofs, and that each proof uses a specific hypothesis (uniform continuity, monotonicity, boundedness) to make U - L small.

divide.name: Properties of the integral
divide.brief: This part proves the algebraic and order properties of the Riemann integral: linearity (integrability of f + g and cf, with the integral of the sum as the sum of integrals), monotonicity (f <= g implies the integral of f is at most the integral of g), additivity over intervals (f integrable on [a,b] if and only if on [a,c] and [c,b], with the integrals adding) and the convention for reversed limits, integrability of |f| and the triangle inequality for integrals, integrability of the composition of an integrable function with a continuous function, and from it integrability of f^2 and of products fg. It ends with the mean value theorem for integrals (for continuous f, and the weighted form with a nonnegative g), using the intermediate and extreme value theorems. Edges: the definition and the Riemann criterion come from 'Darboux sums and the definition of integrability'; integrability of continuous and monotone functions comes from 'Which functions are integrable'. The fundamental theorem of calculus is the next sibling. Interchanging limits and integrals for sequences of functions belongs to 'Sequences and series of functions'. What matters for this learner: these are theorems, not rules, and each proof is a short exercise in working with sup, inf and the Riemann criterion; the composition result is the hardest and shows why it needs continuity of the outer function.

divide.name: The fundamental theorem of calculus and its consequences
divide.brief: This part proves both parts of the fundamental theorem of calculus in full. First, for integrable f, the function F(x) = integral from a to x of f is (Lipschitz) continuous, and is differentiable with F'(c) = f(c) at every point c where f is continuous. Second, if F is differentiable on [a,b] with an integrable derivative F' (not necessarily continuous), then the integral of F' from a to b is F(b) - F(a), proved with the mean value theorem on each subinterval of a partition. Examples showing why the hypotheses matter (a jump in f giving a corner in F; a differentiable function whose derivative is not integrable, mentioned). Consequences proved as theorems with stated hypotheses: integration by parts, integration by substitution (change of variables), and Taylor's theorem with the integral form of the remainder, compared with the Lagrange form. Edges: the mean value theorem, the chain rule, the product rule and Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder come from 'Differentiation' and are used, not reproved. Properties of the integral such as additivity and the mean value theorem for integrals come from 'Properties of the integral'. Computational integration drills are out of scope. When a function equals its Taylor series belongs to 'Sequences and series of functions'. What matters for this learner: the fundamental theorem is a theorem that links this part to 'Differentiation', with precise hypotheses in each half, and the learner should be able to reproduce both proofs and say what fails when a hypothesis is dropped.

divide.name: Improper integrals and the integral test
divide.brief: This part extends the integral beyond bounded functions on closed bounded intervals: improper integrals over unbounded intervals (integral from a to infinity as a limit of integrals over [a,b]) and of functions unbounded near an endpoint, both defined as limits of ordinary Riemann integrals. Convergence and divergence, the standard examples 1/x^p on [1, infinity) and on (0,1], the comparison test for nonnegative integrands, and absolute versus conditional convergence of improper integrals (sin(x)/x as the example, mentioned or proved). The integral test for series with a positive decreasing function, proved by comparing the series with upper and lower sums, with the p-series as the main application and the error estimate for the tail of the series. Edges: series of numbers, the comparison tests for series and the Cauchy condensation test belong to 'Series of real numbers'; this part only adds the integral test and may note that it gives a second proof of the p-series result. Evaluating integrals uses the fundamental theorem from the previous sibling. Lebesgue integration and the gamma function are not treated. What matters for this learner: an improper integral is a limit, not a new kind of integral, so its convergence must be proved; and the integral test is a theorem about comparing sums with integrals, not a recipe.
